# UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (RAP)


The RAP platform serves three complementary purposes: storage, compute, and resource management. 

Users can interact with RAP via a browser-based interface (GUI) or a shell-based interface (CLI).

In principle, users pay a fixed fee for the management (fee paid to have access instated) and the storage of data provided by UK Biobank. They pay a fixed rate (per GB per month) for the storage of data created by the users and a varying sum for the compute they use.

## Accessing RAP

To access the research analysis platform you will need to have an existing UK Biobank account with an approved UK Biobank application ID.

Read this introduction to understand the platform and access requirements: [`https://dnanexus.gitbook.io/uk-biobank-rap`](https://dnanexus.gitbook.io/uk-biobank-rap)

This is a brief description of the process required to set up an account:

- First, setup a profile on the **A**ccess **M**anagement **S**ystem (`ams.ukbiobank.ac.uk`)  
1. Sign up using an institutional email; select a username and a password;   
2. Once your account is approved, update your portfolio and add required info including DOB.  
3. Finish all required online training courses. Use the links provided in your AMS profile page so they get accredited.  
4. Ask your institution to add you to an application and a project under that application.  
5. Confirm that you have been approved both as a user and a project member. This will appear at the end of your AMS profile.

- Now go to the **R**esearch **A**nalysis **P**latform (`ukbiobank.dnanexus.com` )

1. Sign up to RAP. To keep things simple, use the same name, username and email you used on AMS; Follow the instructions provided upon first login to link your account to AMS, set up two-factor authentication with Okta.  
2. Once logged in, you will see that the platform has four main tabs: **Projects; Tools; Organizations; Help**. The landing page is the projects page.

![][image1]

3. The list of projects available to you will appear under your Projects tab, which is the landing page when you login. Each analysis project has  a copy of the UK Biobank data (what we referred to as the 2nd layer in the introduction above). Each project is associated with a billing account, typically your institution’s billing account (company credit card). At first log in, this page will likely be empty. Once you are added to an institutional billing account (done by your PI or the admin for your institution), ask your admin to add you to an existing analysis project as a contributor or create your own analysis project to get your first copy of the UK Biobank data.

![][image2]

4. New users get free credit of £40, which will appear under their personal billing account. This is enough for exploring the platform. You may also use a credit card to continue using your personal account once you have exhausted your credit. For formal analysis, you will have to be added to an organization to access their billing account (ask your PI or platform admin). This will appear under your organizations:

![][image3]






## Understanding data storage layers

There are three layers of data storage and management in the UK Biobank:

- Main depot: this is the central reserve that is accessible only to the UK Biobank team. Researchers do not access this layer directly but will get their own copy (detailed below). Most (text-based) data is stored in databases (SQL); other elements are stored in “no-query” generic or specialized formats. Across all data elements, each participant gets a unique anonymous sample id but this identifier is not used outside of the central depot of UK Biobank data. Each instrument of measurement (e.g, age, sex, etc) gets a unique ‘field id’. This includes genetic data, for instance, genotypes or exomes from a specific pipeline. With each UK Biobank update, fields may be changed or new fields may be added. Details on currently available data are accessible through the [‘Showcase’](https://biobank.ndph.ox.ac.uk/showcase/).  

- Application-specific depot: When you make an application, you will be able to start analysis projects under that application. This process is managed through the [Research Analysis Platform](http://ukbiobank.dnanexus.com). You can start several analysis projects within each application. Each project usually encapsulates an analysis idea but users can decide how to organize their work. Inside RAP, each analysis project is going to get a 'mapping file' to the central databases (that allows the user to query the databases of the central depot), along with a copy of the rest of the UK Biobank data (Bulk directory, contains data not stored in SQL databases but present in other formats like imaging and genetics). The field identifiers remain constant, however, the observations and measurements are ‘dispensed’ to your analysis project(s) with application-specific sample identifiers (i.e. shared across your analysis projects as long as they are under the same application but different than other projects). There is no cost to creating an analysis project per se but users pay for storing the data they create or upload. These project specific data will live as long as the application is active. When your application is concluded, it will be deleted unless you make arrangements with UKBiobank to the contrary. 

- Job-specific depot: the UK Biobank research analysis platform is powered by [DNANexus](https://www.dnanexus.com/) and provides most of the functionalities of the [DNANexus platform](https://documentation.dnanexus.com/) by default. The platform allows users to “rent” AWS-style virtual machines with specific resources for computational analysis. These requests are submitted as jobs on the platform; to run an analysis, users submit jobs to request virtual machines with a pre-specified set of cores, memory, and storage (SSD or HDD) for a given time period (typically hours but can be minutes or days). There is a wide range of virtual machines to choose from and a wide range of specifications; you can rent “vanilla” machines with just a clean Ubuntu Linux that you can then customize (e.g, install your software) or machines with a pre-specified and pre-installed set of tools (e.g, Rstudio, Jupyter Notebook). You can also rent several machines in a SPARK cluster. In any case, these virtual machines have their separate storage; users need to download (“dispense”) data from the storage attached to their analysis project (the 2nd layer above) to the storage attached to these virtual machine; similarly, any new data created during the analysis will be specific to that job, and will be lost once the session ends; results need to be uploaded back to the 2nd layer if the goal is to retain them. Unlike the 2nd storage layer where users pay for the storage they use, here users pay for the storage they request even if not used; a machine with 250GB of SSD storage is going to be more expensive than another one with 100GB SSD or 250GB HDD. 



## Understanding access and resource management

There are two ways to access and manage your project data and computation resources:

- Browser-based user interface (UI): You can manage your data, submit jobs, and do several analysis through RAP website itself. There are dedicated tools for commonly-performed analysis as well tools for basic visualizations. Most tools on the platform (called apps) have a graphical interface that allows users to select input files and select or type in the options for their analysis.

- Shell-based access (CLI): You can do the same as above using the command-line e.g., from your laptop/desktop or HPC (or from a virtual machine rented through DNANexsus itself).

In general, DNANexus toolkit controls the communication between you and your data layers explained above. Therefore it is technically possible to do almost everything from the command line but the web-based GUI offers much more convenience. In the background, both interfaces leverage a set of libraries and APIs from the DNANexus toolkit SDK. 

DX client is one tool from this 'SDK' that offers versatile utilities to manage resrouces, transfer and query data or submit jobs from the terminal. DX client is available in different flavors (e.g., shell-based “dx” and python-based “dxpy”) and can be installed on any machine. From that machine, you will be able to log-in to UK RAP and do your thing. You can build your own apps so you (or others) can use the graphical interface or automate tasks.  



## RAP Projects

Inside RAP, data and analyses are ideally organized under different ‘projects’. These are basically ‘directories’ to organize your work. Each project represents a set of users and files. You could think of an analysis project as a directory linked to a set of users. This is different from what a ‘UKB project’ means under the Access Management System (there, it has to do with your institution’s UKB application). 

You can create your own analysis projects (you will be admin) or ask to be added to an existing project (the admin is usually the analyst who created the analysis project on RAP, not necessarily the PI). As shown above, the projects will appear when you login or when you click on ‘Projects’ at the top of the page.

### New projects

1. Each approved user linked to an application can create a project by clicking on ‘**\+ New Project**’ on the projects page. They will then be the ‘Admin’ of that analysis project. This is different to the ‘Admin’ of the organization who can handle billing and add new members to the organization.  
2. The project admin can then add more members either as ‘Viewers’, ‘Contributors’, or ‘Admins’.   
   1. ‘Admins’ will be able to add other people and make changes to the project itself (description, data, billing, etc). A project can have several admins.   
   2. Collaborators working on the same ‘idea’ will often be added as ‘Contributors’ who can both read and write to the project directory.   
   3. Viewers are typically other analysts in your organization or other organizations who would like to use some of your results for their own work (thus they require read-only rights).   
3. Before running any analyses under a new project you created, remember to add your designated institutional admin to the project as a second project admin and transfer the billing responsibility to them.

### Existing projects

There is a sharing link on the right hand side of the project page where admins can add users to an existing project. See below.


### Project interface


When you double-click on a project, four tabs will appear: **Settings, Manage, Monitor, Visualize**. These four tabs serve management and exporation purposes to different degrees. On the right-hand side, the platform will indicate the type of access you have (Admin, Contributor, Viwer). Next to that, there is a small **shortcut to add new members** if you are allowed to do so.


In brief:
1. Settings is where you can edit the project information, manage billing, and dispense data.  
2. Manage will give you an overview of your data directories and files. This includes data dispensed by UKB and other directories and files created by the project members.  
3. Monitor will show a list of ongoing and past job submissions.  
4. Visualize contains links to IGV, a notebook viewer, and a gzipped file viewer.


![][image4]
 

The contents of the page will update below the tabs when you click on one of them. 'Manage' will act as a file manager (like Finder in Mac or File Explorer in Windows). When active (see image above), it shows a directory tree on the left hand side, the contents of the current directory in the middle, and two links on the right hand side: a link to ‘Add’ items and another link to ‘Start Analysis’. ‘Add’ allows you to create new subdirectories, upload files from your local machine or through a web link, among other things. Start Analysis will give you a list of all apps and applets in your project (see documentation on apps and applets). This includes your own apps/applets as well as those from UKB. In this sense, Start analysis will allow you to start using RAP as a 'compute' platform. Any tools you run will appear under 'Monitor'. 


Inside 'Manage', text files (small ones) can be opened by clicking on them. 'Visualize' will allow you to visualize three other file formats (gz compressed text, bam files via IGV, and notebooks). If you click on a RAP tool that you designed, you will be able to run it. 


It is also possible to browse an analysis project directory using [DX client](https://documentation.dnanexus.com/getting-started/cli-quickstart). E.g., `dx ls` will list the files and directories in the root directory of an analysis project; Tools can be run using `dx run`.



## Contents of an analysis project


When you request access to UK Biobank data through an application, the UK Biobank will ‘dispense’ these through the ‘Data’ platform. This process entails the admin providing details about access control, other users and billing, etc. It is typically done once but you can get ‘updates’ to the data you received whenever they are made available by UK Biobank.


By creating an analysis project, you initiate the 'dispensing' process. When created, RAP projects will have:
- An SQL database.
- An accompaying dataset file.
- A ‘Bulk’ directory. 

These will appear under 'Manage'. UK Biobank stores information in SQL databases which you can query from your project. The dataset and database files are used to link the individuals to their IDs and entries (measurements). For example, they are needed to pull available measurements for your samples in a tabular format (Age, height, IQ, PCs, etc). 

Several other items of UKB data are dispensed under the ‘Bulk’ directory (e.g, ECG, imaging, genetic data) and you don't need to query them. Genetic and imaging data will have to be dispensed after an analysis project is created. Once your data is dispensed for a new project, go to settings; scroll down to dispense data; select dispense more data, and select WES/WGS/etc as required. The data will apear then under `/Bulk`.  


Note the following:
  1. When an analysis project is created, UKB creates unique sample identifiers that are specific to the UKB application under which the analysis project was created. Analysis projects created under the same application will have the same set of sample identifiers, however, these will be different from IDs used for projects created under different applications to maximise anonymity.  
  2. The identifiers will match those in your dataset files but not those in other applications. That means, if you have different pieces of UKB data under different applications, you will have to contact UKB to give you an ID mapping (matching) table.  
  3. You will be notified of updates to UKB data under the ‘Settings’ tab. Updates may change the file names and directory structure under the Bulk directory. If you do not want that, start a new analysis project instead.  
  4. With every update from UKB, a new dataset file will appear (i.e., projects that have existed for a while will have a couple of ‘dataset’ files with time stamps). This ensures that you are using the most up-to-date set of samples and measurements (e.g., it ensures that individuals who dropped are excluded).  
  5. The files on the data platform will remain live as long as your application is active. Once concluded, they will be deleted or archived (unless you arrange with UK Biobank for something different).
  6. You do not pay to access or browse the data platform, nor do you pay for the storage space required to keep UK Biobank data (several petabytes). However, you will have to pay for the storage of your own files including those you created (e.g., outputs from your analysis) or uploaded (e.g., annotations you uploaded to the platform).



## RAP as a cloud computing platform

As a compute platform, RAP will provide you with a set of time-bound resources (cores, memory and disk space) that you can use to perform the analysis you want. This is powered by AWS-style virtual machines (VM). Each request to run compute is called a ‘job’. Jobs will be scheduled based on the priority you give them, which will be reflected in their cost. Ongoing 'compute' will appear under the 'Monitor' tab, which shows logs of cost and time spent running a certain job. Each job will start with a Ubuntu Linux virtual machine that has the requested CPUs, memory, and disk space. The CPUs and RAM will be freed once the job is done. The storage (ssd/hdd) associated with this virtual machine is also time-limited. It will be empty when the machine starts and it will be ‘destroyed’ once the job finishes running. 

RAP uses 'tools' to handle most compute requests. Rather than asking for a 'VM' directly from the GUI/CLI, the VMs are typically requested indirectly by running a single tool (which can be an application or or applet) or a collection of tools in a workflow (outputs from one tool act as inputs for the next one). These requests can be submitted via the GUI and/or the CLI depending on the tool you are using. The tools/applications will fire up a virtual linux machine, run the code they are supposed to run (or the code you provide), and destroy the machine when the work is finished, saving what you ask them to save to a destination of your choosing on the analysis project directory (these outputs will appear there under the 'Manage' tab after the job has finished successfully).  

Since the storage platforms associated with your project and with your VM are technically separate, you (or the tool you are running) will need to do one of the following to have access to your input files:

- Transfer (‘download’) the data you need for your analysis from the ‘Data’ platform to the temporary disk associated with the virtual machine created for the job you submitted.

- Mount the ‘Analysis Project’ storage as a disk on your virtual machine to be able to read it.

Once you are  done with your analysis, you (or the tool you are running) will need to upload any outputs you would like to keep back to the ‘Analysis Project’ storage. Otherwise they will be lost when the virtual machine is destroyed. This concept is key when designing your own tools or when working interactively. 

There are several tools that are available to all users, which are accessible in two ways:

- Click on 'Tools' at the top of the RAP page, then select 'Tools Library'.
- Click on 'Projects', select an analysis project which will automaically open 'Manage' as a landing page, then select 'Start Analysis' (next to 'Add' on the right-hand side of the four sub-panels (Setting, Manage, Monitor, Visualize).

You will have to request resources every time you want to run an analysis via a tool or a workflow, however, most tools have default values in case you do not explicitly indicate your requests. For example, the runtime of the workcloud app is set to one hour by default.

The requested (scheduled, ongoing, finished) jobs will appear under your ‘Monitor’ tab, which will also show the cost you have incurred. The cost depends on what you request, the priority, and the time you requested. You can have a general idea about available resources and their cost by [looking at the rate card](https://20779781.fs1.hubspotusercontent-na1.net/hubfs/20779781/Product%20Team%20Folder/Rate%20Cards/BiobankResearchAnalysisPlatform_Rate%20Card_Current.pdf).

Depending on what you indicate when you run tools, the requested resources will be made available to you (or more precisely, the tool) at a certain priority:

- High priority (will not be interrupted once available). Ideal for interactive work like Rstudio.  
- Low (can be interrupted several times). Ideal for applications that run for a short time.  
- Normal (can be interrupted once). For tools that run for longer periods.

You can communicate with the virtual machine started by your tool using the ‘Monitor’ tab on the RAP platform (using the web browser), or through the command line via DX client. The GUI will typically show a log only (standard error and standard output streams). DX client allows you to check the status of your virtual machine by printing stdout/stderr logs on the screen, or via full ssh access if this was enabled by the tool.

The virtual machine started by the tool will communicate with the RAP platform using the DX client, e.g., to download inputs at the beginning. In this sense, the virtual machine started by the tool behaves like what you would have done had you worked locally (you would have downloaded the data to your desktop to be able to work with it) but within the secure environment provided by DNANexus platform. If there are outputs to save, it will upload them at the end using DX client too.



## Available RAP Tools

There are several ways to run analysis on RAP. Several programs and software are available as tools. DNANexus provides two ways to package software and programs as tools intended for use on their platform: Apps and Applets. Applets are ‘small apps’ or ‘miniature apps’ that are ideal as wrappers to package scripts and binaries with additional instructions on how they should run on the platform. Apps are the same, just more final; these are mature products and cannot be deleted but you can create new versions of the same app.

At the top of UKB-RAP landing page, you will find three links to access apps made available by UKB (read more about the [Tools Library here](https://dnanexus.gitbook.io/uk-biobank-rap/working-on-the-research-analysis-platform/running-analysis-jobs/tools-library)):

- Jupyter Notebook.  
- Rstudio.  
- More tools, which will take you to another page with a list of available tools. A few examples of these tools are:  
  - Cloud Workstation: command-line based ssh access to the compute platform.  
  - Ttyd: web-based access to the compute platform.  
  - URL fetcher: an app to download data to the data platform 

You can create your own tools and save them as ‘applets’ in your project or publish them as full apps.

When you click on a project, you will see a button to ‘Start Analysis’. This will also show you a list of available apps and applets.
